lesson_title: Cryptojacking: Mining Malware and Its Proceeds

metadata.note: No assigned reading for this lesson; every question is grounded in a visible slide.

lectures.title: Cryptojacking: Mining Malware and Its Proceeds - lesson synthesis

questions.question_stem: A company's servers slow to a crawl and its cloud bill triples. An analyst is told the cause is cryptojacking. What did the attacker take from the company?
questions.correct_answer: Electricity and processor time, which the attacker turned into new coins paid to the attacker's own wallet.
incorrect_answers: The company's coins, moved out through a spending permission that its own staff had unknowingly approved.
The company's wallet keys, used to sign a transfer of the company's whole balance to the attacker.
A ransom payment, sent by the company to an address that the attacker named in a note to the company.
questions.explanation: Cryptojacking is mining on someone else's machine without consent. The victim pays for the power and the attacker collects the reward. No victim coins move, which is what separates it from ransomware.
questions.lesson_block: Cryptojacking steals computing power, not coins

specific_source.anchor: Cryptojacking steals computing power, not coins

questions.question_stem: An attacker controls 2,000 hijacked laptops. Why is Monero a better choice than Bitcoin for them to mine?
questions.correct_answer: Monero's mining algorithm is built for ordinary CPUs, so stolen laptops can compete, and its payouts are hidden.
incorrect_answers: Monero can be mined only on hijacked machines, so no legitimate miner would be able to compete with them.
Monero has no mining pools, so no pool operator can ban the attacker's wallet once the malware is found.
Monero mining needs no electricity from the victim, so the hijacked laptops show no slowdown at all to their owners.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin mining is dominated by ASICs, so a hijacked CPU earns almost nothing there. Monero's RandomX is designed for general-purpose CPUs, and Monero hides receiver and amount, so the proceeds start dark.
questions.lesson_block: Most cryptojacking mines Monero, on CPUs

specific_source.anchor: Most cryptojacking mines Monero, on CPUs

questions.question_stem: An agent asks, "How much did the victim pay the cryptojacker?" What is the accurate answer from the chain?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing: the coins are newly mined rewards, so the victim's loss is power and computing time, measured off chain.
incorrect_answers: The total the attacker's wallet received, because every payout to it is money that came from the victim's machines.
The amount in the first transaction into the wallet, because that is where the victim's payment lands on the chain.
It cannot be answered until the pool's payouts are matched to the victim's own wallet addresses by the analyst team.
questions.explanation: In ransomware the victim's payment is the first hop on chain. In cryptojacking the first money is a block reward, a new coin with no earlier owner. Nothing on chain points back to the victim.
questions.lesson_block: No victim pays: the money starts as new coin

specific_source.anchor: No victim pays: the money starts as new coin

questions.question_stem: A pool payout to a wallet looks the same on chain whether the miner's hardware was bought or stolen. What ties the wallet to a crime, then?
questions.correct_answer: Off-chain evidence, such as a malware report or seized machine showing the wallet in the miner's settings.
incorrect_answers: The payout pattern on chain, because stolen hardware always produces payouts at irregular intervals of time.
The size of the payouts, because stolen machines earn less than machines the owner bought for mining.
The pool's identity alone, because only criminals mine through a public pool instead of mining solo.
questions.explanation: The link between wallet and intrusion is off chain: the wallet is typed into the malware as the pool login. The chain shows only a miner being paid, so the typology rests on the malware.
questions.lesson_block: No victim pays: the money starts as new coin

specific_source.anchor: No victim pays: the money starts as new coin

questions.question_stem: A malware report names a Monero wallet and a pool. The ledger hides Monero payouts. What can the analyst still quote about the wallet's earnings?
questions.correct_answer: The pool's own statistics for the wallet, cited as the pool's records with the date they were read.
incorrect_answers: The wallet's balance on the Monero ledger, which any explorer shows alongside the payout history.
The payouts traced one by one to the exchange that received them, using the same methods as for Ether.
Nothing, because Monero hides receiver and amount and pools do not publish figures for any wallet.
questions.explanation: Many pools show the total paid to a wallet and its hashrate, even for Monero. That is a pool's record, not the chain, so it is cited as such, and it is dated because pool pages change and some show only recent payments.
questions.lesson_block: The wallet in the sample is the pivot

specific_source.anchor: The wallet in the sample is the pivot

questions.question_stem: The same wallet turns up in 40 mining samples from campaigns that otherwise share nothing. What is the likeliest explanation?
questions.correct_answer: It is a donation wallet that a stock mining tool pays a small share to, not one attacker's wallet.
incorrect_answers: It belongs to the largest pool, which every campaign has to use in order to be paid its mining rewards.
It is one attacker running 40 campaigns, because a wallet repeated across samples groups them as one actor.
It is the victims' shared wallet, because the samples were all collected from machines at one company.
questions.explanation: Same wallet across samples normally groups samples into one campaign, but stock mining tools mine a share for their developer. A wallet in many unrelated campaigns is the known false positive, so donation wallets are screened out before grouping.

questions.question_stem: A wallet earned 40 XMR from a cloud cryptojacking campaign. The victim's cloud bill for the same period was $200,000. What does the analyst report as the victim's loss?
questions.correct_answer: The $200,000 bill, from the victim's records, with the wallet's earnings reported separately as earnings.
incorrect_answers: The value of the 40 XMR, because the attacker's earnings are the measure of what the victim lost in all.
The $200,000 minus the value of the 40 XMR, because the attacker's coins offset part of the bill.
Neither figure, because a loss can only be stated once the miner is removed from every machine in use.
questions.explanation: Sysdig estimated $53 billed for every $1 an attacker earned in one group's campaign. The coins understate the harm, and the loss figure comes from the victim, not the chain.
questions.lesson_block: In the cloud the victim pays the bill

specific_source.anchor: In the cloud the victim pays the bill

questions.question_stem: Browser mining and cloud cryptojacking both end in coins for the attacker. Which difference matters most to a victim once the miner is found?
questions.correct_answer: Closing a browser tab ends the mining, but closing a hijacked cloud account leaves the bill already run up.
incorrect_answers: Browser mining needs a malware file on the visitor's disk, while cloud mining runs without any software.
Cloud mining always pays out in Monero, while browser mining pays out only in public-ledger coins.
Browser mining is reported under a different ATT&CK technique, so the victim cannot recover any costs at all.
questions.explanation: A web-page miner stops when the visitor leaves the site. In the cloud the accounts are opened or taken under false pretenses, and closing them does not cancel the charges.
questions.lesson_block: Cryptojacking: mining on someone else's machine

questions.question_stem: In the Parks case, the attacker mined Ether, Litecoin and Monero and cashed out through exchanges, an NFT marketplace, a payment provider and banks. Which legs can the chain itself show?
questions.correct_answer: The Ether and Litecoin payouts, and the exits to the exchanges and the NFT marketplace.
incorrect_answers: All of the legs, because every exit started from a payout recorded on a public ledger.
The Monero payouts and the payment and bank legs, because they hold the most value.
Only the exchange exits, because the marketplace and payouts leave no public record.
questions.explanation: Ether and Litecoin are transparent, so their payouts and on-chain exits show. Monero is hidden, and the account-opening, payment-provider and bank legs can only come from those firms' records.
questions.lesson_block: Parks: a cloud bill over three times the coin

questions.question_stem: An analyst calls a wallet "cryptojacking proceeds" because it receives steady pool payouts. What is wrong with that finding?
questions.correct_answer: A payout looks like any miner's, so it needs off-chain evidence and a stated alternative.
incorrect_answers: Pool payouts only occur for legitimate mining, so they count as evidence against cryptojacking.
The finding needs a victim payment on chain, because without one the wallet cannot be linked.
Nothing is wrong, because steady payouts to one wallet are the defining on-chain sign of it.
questions.explanation: On chain a cryptojacker's payout is the same as a legitimate miner's. An honest note states the typology, the evidence for and against, and at least one other explanation, such as a donation wallet or a legitimate miner.

questions.question_stem: An analyst has found one wallet in a malware sample and rates the wallet-to-campaign link Moderate. Which new evidence would justify High?
questions.correct_answer: The pool's own logs showing that wallet's login mining from the victims' machines.
incorrect_answers: Five more samples of the same malware family that contain the same wallet again.
A second malware report on the same sample that repeats the first report's wallet.
A pool ban of the wallet that followed the researchers' report on the same malware.
questions.explanation: High needs two independent lines, meaning a different kind of evidence. More samples of the same malware are the same kind, and a ban prompted by the same report is not independent. The pool's records are a different kind.

questions.question_stem: A limits-of-tracing note on a Monero mining wallet reaches the pool's payouts. How should the note record that step?
questions.correct_answer: As the stop: Monero hides receiver and amount, so no address or amount is quoted and the trail resumes at a transparent coin.
incorrect_answers: As a Low-confidence link: the payouts are traced to the likeliest exchange by their timing and amount alone, as the note puts it.
As a continuation: the wallet's pool total is treated as the traced amount for the next hop in the flow of funds.
As an error: the note should leave out any step that the ledger does not let the analyst follow at all in it, so it ends.
questions.explanation: The note starts at the wallet, stops at the Monero payouts, and keeps the leads that remain. If the same campaign also mined a transparent coin such as Ether, its payouts to an exchange deposit address reopen the trail.

questions.question_stem: A company's blocklist of mining-pool domain names shows no hits, yet a miner is running on its servers. Which explanation does the lesson give?
questions.correct_answer: The attacker's own subdomain is a DNS alias that resolves to the pool, so a list of pool names misses it.
incorrect_answers: The miner talks to no pool at all, because Monero is mined alone and never reports to any pool.
The blocklist is checked against Bitcoin pools only, so a Monero pool's name is never compared to it at all.
The pool banned the company's address, so the miner's connection is dropped before any name appears.
questions.explanation: A CNAME is a DNS alias: the attacker's subdomain resolves to the real pool, so a blocklist of pool names misses it. The pool's own records still show the wallet logging in.
